absent: Real regulator backend behavior when support is enabled is not shown.
Relay sub-buffer switch, open, close and reader-side consumption protocol beyond inline helpers is not shown.
Architecture resource accessor, resctrl schema, group and monitor-domain structures beyond headers are not shown.
Locking and concurrency rules for regulator and resctrl objects are not shown.
Numeric error code values and BIT macro expansion are not defined in these fragments.

findings.text: Regulator operating modes are encoded as distinct small integers: invalid is zero, fast is one, normal is two, idle is four and standby is eight, allowing bitmask combination except for invalid.

Regulator error and warning indicators are single-bit flags occupying bit positions one through nine in ascending order: under-voltage, over-current, regulation-out, fail and over-temperature for errors, plus under-voltage warn, over-current warn, over-voltage warn and over-temperature warn for warnings.
Pre-change notification payload carries three unsigned long microvolt quantities representing the previous level and the requested minimum and maximum bounds.
Bulk consumer descriptor pairs a supply name string with a consumer handle and an initial load in microamps, plus a private integer for per-entry status used internally.

In the configured stub variant the plain and device-managed shared acquisition helpers always yield a null handle, signaling absence of regulator support while remaining safe for drivers that skip further calls.
Exclusive, optional and device-tree optional acquisition helpers in the stub variant always report missing device, indicating no regulator instance can be obtained.
Device-managed combined get-and-enable helpers for the shared and optional cases report success without action, while the read-voltage combined helper reports missing device.

Stub power-control, bulk and alias operations are no-ops reporting success: enables, disables, forced disable, deferred disable, bulk get, bulk enable, bulk disable, bulk forced disable, supply-alias registration and notifier registration all return zero, bulk free and put helpers do nothing, and the enabled query always reports true.

Stub measurement and configuration queries use fixed sentinel results: voltage set, voltage-time, current-limit set, mode set, load set and bypass allow report success with no effect, supported-voltage check and linear step and current limit and voltage count return zero, voltage and suspend and list operations report invalid argument, regmap and hardware-select operations report unsupported, power-budget request reports unsupported while unclaimed budget reports maximum integer, error-flag query reports invalid, mode query reports normal, and driver-data get yields null.

Triplet and tolerance voltage helpers attempt a narrow target window first and fall back to a wider window on failure; the tolerance support check delegates to the supported-voltage query over the expanded interval around the target.

Bulk supply-name assignment does nothing, regulator identity comparison always reports not equal, and device-tree bulk retrieval for all supplies reports success without populating details in the stub variant.

Ignore-region skip helper advances a copy cursor without storing: it does nothing when no bytes remain, requires the current position not to precede the region start, and when the region end is negative or ahead it consumes up to the remaining count or up to the region end, advancing the kernel or user source pointer accordingly and updating position and remaining count.

User-to-regset copy entry validates that the selected set provides a write handler and that the user range is accessible, then forwards target, descriptor, offset, size and user address to that handler with no kernel staging buffer.
Relay channel version identifier has value seven.
Relay buffer statistics flags use bit zero for buffer-full and bit one for write-too-large, with the last-defined marker equal to the write-too-large flag.
Per-buffer statistics record holds two unsigned counters, one for buffer-full events and one for oversized-write events.

Relay per-CPU buffer descriptor begins with channel memory anchors and progress markers: start of allocation, current sub-buffer base, offset within current sub-buffer, counts of produced and consumed sub-buffers, back-pointer to channel, reader wait queue, deferred wakeup work and file representation.

Relay per-CPU buffer descriptor continues with lifetime and paging state: reference count, embedded statistics, page array and page count, finalized flag, per-sub-buffer padding array, consumed-byte counts for current and early phases, and owning CPU number; the whole record is cache-line aligned.

Relay channel descriptor starts with sizing and linkage: version number, sub-buffer size, sub-buffer count, total allocated size, client callback table pointer, reference count and opaque private pointer.

Relay channel descriptor continues with buffer topology and naming: per-CPU buffer pointer table, global-buffer indicator, channel list linkage, parent directory entry, filename-presence flag and stored base filename up to the system name limit.

Client callback table aggregates three operations: a sub-buffer start notifier returning a continuation decision, a buffer-file creation operation returning a directory entry and optionally selecting global buffering, and a buffer-file removal operation returning status.

Sub-buffer start callback is invoked on each switch including initial creation with null previous pointer, returning one to continue and zero to stop, and may reserve leading bytes in the new area; creation and removal callbacks are mandatory and invoked once per per-CPU buffer during open and close.

Inline write helpers append to the current CPU buffer at the current offset, switching sub-buffers when the payload would overflow and truncating length to the switch result; the reserve variant returns a direct pointer into free space or null when no space can be made, advancing the offset on success.

One write path masks local interrupts around current-CPU buffer lookup and update, while the other write and reserve paths pin the current CPU around the same critical section using paired acquire and release helpers.

Relay buffering progresses by offset within a sub-buffer until capacity is reached, at which point a sub-buffer switch is requested and produced and consumed counters track hand-off between writer and reader sides.
Sub-buffer reservation helper sets the buffer offset to a caller-chosen length, requiring that length stay strictly below sub-buffer capacity minus one.
Skipping before its declared start and reserving at or beyond capacity trigger immediate bug checks, so callers must guarantee position and length preconditions.
CPU preparation hook for relay is defined as null, indicating no preparation callback.
Resource-control reserved identifiers for default control group and monitoring group are both zero, and the any-CPU selector is negative one.
Maximum memory-bandwidth allocation value equals the largest 32-bit unsigned integer.

Resource levels enumerate last-level cache, second-level cache, memory-bandwidth allocation, software memory-bandwidth allocation and per-package performance scope in that order, with resource count defined as last index plus one.

Iteration helpers walk all resources via an architecture accessor incrementing the identifier, with filtered variants that skip entries lacking both capabilities, lacking allocation capability, or lacking monitoring capability respectively.
Code-data prioritization types enumerate none, code and data with last equal to data, and the type count is last plus one.
Cache pseudo-lock region begins with schema pointer, class identifier, domain pointer, capacity mask, waiter queue, thread-completion flag and designated CPU.
Cache pseudo-lock region continues with geometry and bookkeeping: line size, total size, kernel memory pointer, minor number, debug directory entry and power-management request list.
Staged configuration pairs a new control value with a boolean indicating whether a new value is pending.
Domain categories distinguish control domains from monitoring domains.

Common domain header links siblings, carries numeric identifier, domain category, resource level and CPU membership mask; a validation helper reports true only when stored category and level match expected values, warning once otherwise.
Control-domain extension embeds the common header, an optional pseudo-lock pointer, a per-type array of staged configurations sized by code-data type count, and a pointer to bandwidth values.
Memory-bandwidth monitoring counter configuration pairs an event identifier with a pointer to the associated resource group.
Header inclusion guards for regulator consumer, relay and resource-control headers are defined to prevent multiple inclusion.
